content.body: Have you ever wondered if a word or phrase reads the same forwards and backwards? That's called a palindrome. Today, we'll learn how to check if a string is a valid palindrome using a clever technique. We'll use a lookup structure to remember what we've already seen.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Apply a two-pointer approach to traverse a string from both ends.
2. Implement a lookup structure to skip non-alphanumeric characters efficiently.
3. Explain why checking characters in pairs is more efficient than creating a reversed copy.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. Look at this string: 'racecar'. Does it read the same forwards and backwards?
content.title: Try it
Try a phrase
content.prompt: Is 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' a palindrome if we ignore spaces, punctuation, and case?
content.successMessage: Great! When cleaned, it becomes 'amanaplanacanalpanama', which is a palindrome.

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Correct! 'hello' is not a palindrome because 'h' != 'o'.

content.body: What you just did was a mental comparison: you looked at characters from both ends and checked if they match. For short strings, this is easy, but for longer strings with mixed characters, it gets tricky.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the string is long and contains spaces, punctuation, or different cases, comparing characters directly becomes messy. We need a method that efficiently skips non-alphanumeric characters and compares only relevant ones. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. We can use a lookup structure (like a Set or a helper function) to quickly check if a character is alphanumeric. This avoids scanning the string multiple times. Think of it as a notebook where we write down the rules for valid characters and check them in one step.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use two pointers: one starting at the beginning (left) and one at the end (right). Move them towards each other, skipping non-alphanumeric characters, and compare the characters at each step. If all pairs match, it's a palindrome.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama':
1. Left='A' (alphanumeric), right='a' (alphanumeric). Lowercase both → 'a' == 'a'. Move pointers.
2. Skip spaces/punctuation as needed.
3. Continue until pointers meet. All pairs match → true.

content.body:
1. Initialize left pointer at index 0 and right pointer at last index.
2. While left < right:
   a. Move left pointer to the next alphanumeric character.
   b. Move right pointer to the previous alphanumeric character.
   c. Compare characters (case-insensitive). If different, return false.
3. If loop finishes, return true.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function skeleton
steps.instruction: Start by creating a function called isPalindrome that takes a string parameter s.
steps.hint: Use the function keyword or an arrow function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function takes one parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function named isPalindrome with parameter s.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, initialize two variables: left starting at 0 and right starting at the last index of the string.
steps.hint: Use s.length to find the last index.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Pointers are ready to traverse from both ends.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Remember to subtract 1 from length for the last index.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax. Initialize left and right as numbers.

steps.title: Set up the main loop
steps.instruction: Create a while loop that continues as long as left is less than right.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good! The loop will run until pointers meet.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. The condition should check left < right.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember, the loop continues while left is less than right.

steps.title: Skip non-alphanumeric characters
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, add two while loops to move left and right pointers past non-alphanumeric characters. Use a helper function or regex to check.
steps.hint: You can use /[a-zA-Z0-9]/ to test alphanumeric.
steps.expectedOutcome:
while (left < right && !/[a-zA-Z0-9]/.test(s[left])) left++;
while (left < right && !/[a-zA-Z0-9]/.test(s[right])) right--;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now pointers will skip invalid characters.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Ensure the conditions check for non-alphanumeric and prevent pointer crossover.
steps.feedbackWrong: Think about using regex test and increment/decrement pointers.

steps.title: Compare characters and return result
steps.instruction: After skipping non-alphanumeric characters, compare the characters at left and right (case-insensitive). If they don't match, return false. Otherwise, move pointers inward and continue. After the loop, return true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Fantastic! You've implemented the complete palindrome checker.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the comparison and pointer movement. Don't forget to return true at the end.
steps.feedbackWrong: Compare characters case-insensitively and move pointers after a match.

content.body: Congratulations! You've learned how to check for valid palindromes using a two-pointer approach with a lookup structure for alphanumeric checks. Remember: use pointers to traverse from both ends, skip non-relevant characters efficiently, and compare case-insensitively. This method is optimal and avoids creating extra strings.
content.title: Done
